title: The Ceasefire Expires: Prelude to the Final Act
content:
When the four-month cessation of hostilities expired on 1 May 1995 without renewal, the resumption of fighting was immediate and violent. Artillery barrages resumed along front lines from the Posavina corridor to Herzegovina. The war that recommenced was not a continuation of the grinding attritional stalemate that had characterized much of 1993 and 1994. It was something qualitatively different — a final phase in which accumulated military preparations, shifting strategic calculations, and hardening international resolve would combine to produce the most dramatic territorial changes of the entire conflict within a span of months.

The strategic landscape had shifted during the ceasefire in ways that were not yet fully visible. The Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina had used the winter to reorganize, retrain, and integrate new equipment. The ARBiH's 7th Corps and elements of the 3rd Corps were better positioned for operations in central Bosnia. The 5th Corps in the Bihac pocket, which had nearly been overrun in November 1994, had consolidated its defenses and maintained coordination with Croatian forces across the border. The Washington Agreement's military dividends were materializing as joint planning between ARBiH and HVO formations advanced.

The VRS, for its part, had used the ceasefire to concentrate forces for operations against the eastern enclaves. As documented in both the ICTY Karadzic Trial Judgment (IT-95-5/18-T) and the Mladic Trial Judgment (IT-09-92-T), the Bosnian Serb political and military leadership had been planning operations against Srebrenica and Zepa during the ceasefire period. The Drina Corps had repositioned units and stockpiled ammunition. The operational concept that would be executed in July 1995 was already taking shape during the winter months.

Beyond the immediate belligerents, Croatia's military transformation was approaching its culmination. The Croatian Army had been reorganized and retrained, and Zagreb was preparing for decisive operations to recapture territories held by the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Operation Flash, launched against Western Slavonia on 1 May 1995 — the very day the ceasefire formally expired — signaled that Croatia was now willing to use force at scale. The implications for the Bosnian Serb strategic position were profound. The VRS had long relied on strategic depth provided by Serb-held territories in Croatia. That depth was about to disappear.

The international context was also evolving. The Bihac crisis and the persistent inability of UNPROFOR to fulfill its mandate had generated intense debate within NATO capitals about the future of the peacekeeping mission. France and Britain, the largest troop contributors, were reassessing their posture. The concept of a rapid reaction force with robust rules of engagement was under active discussion. The United States, which had no ground troops in Bosnia, was moving toward a more assertive diplomatic and military posture under pressure from Congress and the approaching 1996 presidential election.

The expiration of the ceasefire thus marked not merely the resumption of a war that had paused, but the beginning of its terminal phase. The military balance was shifting against the Bosnian Serbs, whose overstretched forces held vast territory but faced an increasingly capable adversary, growing Croatian pressure on their western flank, and an international community moving haltingly but perceptibly toward intervention. The five months between May and October 1995 would produce Srebrenica, Operation Storm, NATO air strikes, and the ground offensive that finally created the conditions for a negotiated settlement at Dayton. None of this was inevitable in late April. But the ingredients were assembled, and the ceasefire's expiration set them in motion.
